As part of what I do for a living, I occasionally have to look up information on various US Federal and State government websites. I have noticed over the last few years on these websites that links to social media have become much more common.

The traditional ways for private citizens to contact their governmental officials have not changed and I don’t think that social media is going to change this over the next few years. I don’t think you will be able to renew a driver’s license over Twitter or supply an official public comment on a draft rule via Facebook anytime soon. The influence of State government social media sites appears to be comparatively small and I don’t anticipate that these social media sites will become relatively large or important anytime soon.

But all that being said, it bothers me to see evidence that social media companies, especially the larger ones, have a persistent political bias. Every time a governmental agency sends out a Tweet or maintains a Facebook page, they are tacitly endorsing a company that has demonstrated a political bias. It is not essential that government be efficient, but it should be fair.

With Voat’s indulgence, I decided to visit the websites of all 50 US States just to document the numbers of social media links. Here are the results. Enjoy.

 

**Homepages**

Number of states with account links to the following social media sites on their homepage:

* Facebook 33 * Twitter 37 * YouTube 20 * Flickr 25 * Vimeo 1 * Pinterest 6 * Instagram 5 * Linked In 5 * Tumblr 0 * Google+ 5 * Other 1

Not all links to social media sites had the same prominence. Some were small icons at the bottom of the page and some were large boxes at the top. Some had prominent Twitter feeds on their homepage (I did not count the exact number but I think it was about 10 – 15).

Delaware had an option to share a link on their homepage, which included over 200 options, none of which was Voat. Vermont had a direct link to share on Digg.

Florida’s official site was the only dot com. There was another Florida site that had a more official-sounding name, but it appeared to be just for Governor Rick Scott.

http://www.myflorida.com/

http://www.flgov.com/

 

**Social Media Pages**

Most states have a dedicated social media page on their websites, which is usually linked directly to their homepage. I found a social media page for 33 of the states. I can’t say that the other 17 states did not have them, just that I couldn’t find them after a brief search.

These social media pages provide a summary of direct social media links for various departments, agencies, and organizations within the respective states. It was hard to compare raw numbers from one state to another because some state social media pages would only show state-level departments whereas others would also include various towns, counties, and state universities. Utah in particular included everything and had 1,720 links, which is why it was excluded in the data below. The 17 states that did not have an apparent dedicated social media page most likely have department-level social media accounts, but I did not tabulate them since they would have been scattered.

Average number of account links to the following social media sites from 32 states:

* Facebook 52 * Twitter 48 * YouTube 23 * Flickr 9 * Vimeo <1 * Pinterest 2 * Instagram 3 * Linked In 3 * Tumblr <1 * Google+ <1 * Other <1

The Other category included a Foursquare link in Iowa: https://foursquare.com/travel_iowa

 

**Search Engines**

Every state website had a dedicated search field, unsurprisingly. I could not tell who/what was the search engine behind 27 of them. For the rest that I could identify, 13 were identified as Google, 9 as Bing, and 1 as Verity. Many sites also had a translation service, and most of them seemed to be powered by Google, however I did not tabulate this.

 

**Request for Location**

Four states asked for my location: Arkansas, Delaware, and Utah from the homepage and Maryland from their social media page. Idaho asked to run Silverlight. Indiana had an ask-a-question box pop up the first time.
